beats.say: JCPenney dropped coupons. And prices stayed high.
Every day they promised "Fair and Square" pricing.
No more flash sales, just the same tags on the shelf.
A single price you could see every visit.
Sales fell 25% and the company lost $985 million - looks catastrophic.
But it fuels the discount feeling, not the price.
Shoppers chase the feeling of a discount, not the low price itself.
The constant-price option became the reference point, making the everyday price seem like a deal.
That illusion slashed sales by a quarter and cost almost a billion dollars.
You see it everywhere: a coffee shop sells a drip for $2, a latte for $4, and a specialty brew for $4.95.
The latte feels cheap next to the specialty, so customers upgrade.
A gym lists basic $30, premium $45, elite $49 - the $45 plan feels smart next to $49.
A cinema shows standard $12, recliner $15, VIP $16 - the recliner becomes the obvious choice.
If a price feels like a discount, check the reference - follow for more.
